title: Sorting and list tools
summary: sort() puts the same list in order, sorted() makes a new sorted list. Plus reverse, count and index.

intro.text:
There are two ways to put a list in order, and the difference matters:

- `xs.sort()` sorts **the same list**. It changes it and gives back **None**
- `sorted(xs)` makes a **new** sorted list and leaves `xs` exactly as it was

Add `reverse=True` inside the brackets of either one to go from biggest to smallest. A `name=value` inside the brackets is a **setting** for the call.

The **refs** panel shows the difference: after `sort()` there is still one list, after `sorted()` there are two.

Numbers sort by size. Text sorts letter by letter, and **every capital comes before every small letter**, so `"Zoe"` comes before `"amy"`.

More tools that only look and never change the list:

- `xs.count(6)`: how many items equal 6
- `xs.index(6)`: the position of the first 6 (an error if there is none)

And `xs.reverse()` flips the list in place, without sorting.
intro.analogy: Sorting a hand of cards. sort() is rearranging the cards in your own hand. sorted() is laying out a second, ordered copy on the table while your hand stays as it was.

mistakes.title: Sorting numbers mixed with text
mistakes.explain: Python cannot tell whether a number is smaller than a piece of text, so it refuses to sort. Keep one kind of value in a list you sort.

gen.error: TypeError: '<' not supported between instances of 'str' and 'int'

mistakes.title: Looking up a value that is not there
mistakes.explain: index stops the program when the value is missing. Check with in first.

gen.error: ValueError: list.index(x): x not in list

mistakes.title: Calling sorted like a method
mistakes.explain: sorted is not a list method. It is a function that takes the list inside its brackets.

gen.error: AttributeError: 'list' object has no attribute 'sorted'. Did you mean: 'sort'?
